title: Eutychus falls asleep (Acts 20:1–16)
hook: Paul preaches till midnight, a young man dozes off in a window, and is restored
carry: they were not a little comforted
tomorrow: Paul's last words to his friends are words of Jesus. which ones?

segments.voice: The Ephesus riot ended when a town clerk told a furious theater: be quiet, do nothing rashly. Paul travels on through Macedonia and Greece, to a crowded upstairs room in Troas.
screen: `BE QUIET, DO NOTHING RASHLY.` → `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM IN TROAS.`

segments.voice: Every teacher knows the sight: a head in the back row dipping, catching itself, dipping again. Maybe you've been that head once or twice. Troas, the first day of the week. The believers have gathered to break bread, and Paul, who leaves in the morning, "continued his speech until midnight." Then Acts adds a detail that seems to go nowhere: "there were many lights in the upper chamber." Why tell us about the lamps? Because a young man is sitting in the window, and he's fading.
screen: `A HEAD IN THE BACK ROW, DIPPING.` → `UNTIL MIDNIGHT.` → `WHY MENTION THE LAMPS?`

segments.voice: "And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead." So, the lamps. Acts never says why it mentions them. Some readers hear a gentle explanation tucked into the scene: a crowded room, many flames, a late hour, a long talk. And look at the phrase as Paul was long preaching. The text practically takes the young man's side. His tiredness isn't treated as a sin. Paul stops. He goes down, throws himself on the young man, and holds him. "Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him." Readers weigh that line differently: some hear a raising from the dead, others hear Paul finding life still there. Either way, see what happens next. Paul goes back up, breaks bread, eats, and keeps talking "a long while, even till break of day." No lecture about staying awake. And the last line goes to the people in the room: "And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted." Here's the one to tell a friend: the young man who nodded off becomes the reason a whole room goes home comforted.
screen: `MANY LIGHTS, A LATE HOUR.` · `AS PAUL WAS LONG PREACHING.` · `HIS LIFE IS IN HIM.` · `TILL BREAK OF DAY.` · then, large: `NOT A LITTLE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the tired people who showed up for you lately: someone who drove you after a long shift, sat through your thing half-asleep, answered a late text. Give each one a finger and a quiet thank-you; tired people who came anyway still came. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.
Eutychus falls asleep. A young man in a window, a sermon past midnight, and a fall that ends in comfort.
Pocket this one: they were not a little comforted, which is old English for a great deal. Sleep well.

howItsDone: Christians read the story of Eutychus in Acts 20; some note that the believers there gathered on the first day of the week to break bread, and some churches point to it when they gather on Sundays.

fork.setup: your grandpa nods off during your sister's piano recital. afterward she's furious and wants you to back her up. what fits Eutychus?
options: remind her gently that he came, and the night was long.
agree he was rude, and say he owes her an apology.
suggest he skip the next one if he's that tired.
fork.reveal: Acts puts the long sermon in the sentence, not blame on the sleeper, and ends with a room not a little comforted.

trapdoor: what you thought: Eutychus is the warning: don't fall asleep in church.
what it means: Acts doesn't scold him; Paul holds him, and the room is not a little comforted.
what a scholar hears: Acts says he was taken up dead, and Paul says his life is in him; some readers hear a raising, others life found still there.

a bishop who stayed up praying all night

chat.says: ran my audition piece for dad. he fell asleep halfway. he just did a 24hr shift. still hurts tho
options: It can hurt and still be forgiven. Acts blames the long sermon, not Eutychus. Dad showed up tired.
Tell him straight out how much it hurt. Paul stopped and scolded Eutychus for nodding off.
Then don't ask him again. After Eutychus fell, they ended the whole meeting early.
chat.meaning: Acts says Eutychus sank down 'as Paul was long preaching', and nobody scolds him; the room ends comforted. Tiredness gets mercy.

Troas.meaning: a port town where the believers gathered

Eutychus.meaning: the young man who fell from the window

break bread.meaning: share a meal; Christians also use it of communion

notes: v3 puzzle shape: the odd detail is 'many lights in the upper chamber' (20:8). The lesson says Acts never explains it and that 'some readers' hear a gentle explanation (a crowded room, many flames, a late hour). Confirm this is fairly hedged.
The teach says readers weigh 'taken up dead' and 'his life is in him' differently (a raising, or life still there). Confirm the framing is fair.
The index hook says 'a boy'; Acts 20:9 says 'a certain young man' and 20:12 'the young man'. The lesson uses 'young man'.
The name Eutychus is often glossed 'fortunate'; that meaning is left out under the claims rule.
'Not a little is old English for a great deal' explains the KJV idiom (litotes). Confirm.
